0d37db2.summary: The Employer stock page now works out the tax your next year of stock vests will bring by running them through the full federal tax estimate, one calendar year at a time, and compares that with what your employer really withholds. The tax on selling shares to bring one company under 10% of your savings is now worked through the real capital-gains rates instead of one flat rate. A big vest can push you into a higher bracket, and the old shortcut could get that bill wrong.
points: Shares that vest (company stock you receive on a schedule, taxed like pay) are added to your other income for each year and taxed through the brackets, including the extra 0.9% Medicare tax on high pay.
The page shows what your employer withholds: 22%, 37% on bonus-type pay past $1 million in a year, and 0.9% for Medicare on pay past $200,000. It also says whether that covers the tax.
The tax on selling down to 10% is worked through the 0%, 15% and 20% gain rates, plus the 3.8% extra tax on investment income.
The page no longer sets a 10% minimum on the tax rate it shows.
numbers: 22% withheld on vests
37% withheld on bonus-type pay past $1 million
0.9% Medicare tax on pay past $200,000
10%: the usual ceiling for one company

shots.caption: The Employer stock page with the sample household: four vests of $6,000 each with $1,320 withheld on each, and about $5,280 of extra federal tax worked year by year. Below that, what selling down toward 10% would cost in tax. This picture already includes the small follow-up change made right after this one: the lines for 2026 and 2027 and the $36,000 of units that already vested this year come from it.

b0c0238.summary: The Rental analysis and Home pages now agree with the property answer key on every figure. The key is an independent program written from the tax law, without reading the app, that worked thousands of example households. Rental losses and the tax on a home sale now follow the real rules, so you see the tax a rental or a sale really adds.
points: Rental: a rental with a profit soaks up your other rentals' losses first. The loss that counts this year and the loss that waits are shared out by the size of each rental's loss.
Rental: a married couple filing separately who lived together gets no allowance (the rule that lets some rental losses come off other income). The tax now includes the 3.8% extra tax on net rent.

Home: the tax-free $250,000 / $500,000 of gain needs two of the last five years owned and lived in. A new box keeps part of it if you sell early because of a new job, your health or something you could not foresee.
Home: a home owned a year or less is taxed like pay. The tax is worked through the federal estimate, and the 3.8% applies only to income over the line.
numbers: 1,500 depreciation rows checked
2,000 households with 3,489 rentals
1,500 home sales
$250,000 / $500,000 of tax-free home gain

shots.caption: The Rental analysis page with two sample rentals. The top now says the losses cancel the profits, so this year's tax does not change, and $19,997 of loss waits for a later year.

The Home page for a home bought in May 2025. It has not yet been owned and lived in for two years (that happens on May 1, 2027), so the whole $57,200 gain is taxed: about $9,987, of which $607 is the 3.8% extra tax.
The home's details on the same page, ending with the new box: selling before two years because of a new job, your health or an event you could not foresee.

a1e8ef9.summary: This built the property answer key, an independent program written from the tax law without reading the app. It works out depreciation, rental losses and home-sale tax for thousands of example households, and a test compares the Rental analysis and Home pages with it. Every figure the pages worked by their own method matched, but the key found nine places where that method differed from the law. They went on a to-do list that the next change fixed.
points: It works 1,500 depreciation rows (the yearly write-off of a rental building), 2,000 households owning 3,489 rentals, and 1,500 home sales.
It is built from the tax law on home sales, depreciation, rental losses and the 3.8% investment-income tax, plus IRS publications and forms.

Rental gaps found: one rental's profit was not netted against another's loss; the loss allowance (the part of a rental loss that can come off other income) was applied in the wrong order, and wrongly for a couple filing separately who lived together; and the tax used one flat rate with no 3.8% on rent.
Home gaps found: no two-of-five-years test, no pay-like rate for a home held a year or less, one flat rate, and the 3.8% charged on the whole gain.
numbers: 1,500 depreciation rows
2,000 households with 3,489 rentals
1,500 home sales
9 differences from the law found

shots.caption: The Rental analysis page before the fixes. The tax on the rental's income used one flat rate ('about $914 of tax at 22%'), a shortcut the answer key flagged.
The Home page as it was. The 'If you sold today' box only compared the gain with the $500,000 tax-free amount and worked out no tax.

574661f.summary: This tightened the Crypto and Tax lots pages after an independent review. Selling everything now applies the wash-sale rule (a loss does not count if you buy the same fund back within 30 days) even when the new purchase is in an IRA. The loss carried to next year now counts the whole carryover, and a sale today is always worked in today's tax year. For a couple filing separately, a sale now goes on the return of the spouse who owns it.
points: If a fund sold at a loss was bought again within 30 days in an IRA, that part of the loss now counts for nothing, as the law says.
The loss carried to next year looks at the whole carryover, so a gain of one kind can use up a carried loss of the other kind.
A sale today is worked in this year's taxes even when the Federal estimate is set to another year.
Filing separately, a sale can say whose it is and goes on that spouse's own return. The Crypto page also says the yearly loss limit is $1,500 for separate filers.
The Crypto page now treats a bitcoin fund held in a crypto account as a fund, shows the day each purchase turns long-term, and explains when the tax does not change.
numbers: 30-day wash-sale window
$1,500 yearly loss limit filing separately

shots.caption: The Crypto page with a sample wallet. Each purchase now says when it turns long-term (for example 'long-term from Dec 6, 2026'), and 'If you sold everything today' explains the extra federal tax after losses cancel gains.

8ea373f.summary: The Crypto page's three tax figures now come from the full federal tax estimate instead of a single rate: the tax if you sold today, the saving from banking a loss, and the saving from waiting for the lower long-term rate. Losses first cancel this year's gains, only $3,000 comes off pay, and the rest carries to next year, so the savings shown are realistic.
points: The tax if you sold is the federal tax with the coins sold minus the tax without, so it reflects your real bracket.
A net loss takes at most $3,000 off other income this year. The rest carries forward the way the IRS worksheet does it.
A bitcoin or ether fund bought again within 30 days, in any account including an IRA, cancels the loss on that many shares (the wash-sale rule), and the page names the purchase.
The page no longer sets a 10% minimum on the rate shown, and the Digital estate link is now a full-size button.
numbers: $3,000 of loss a year off other income
30-day wash-sale window

shots.caption: The Crypto page with a sample wallet. Selling everything adds about $1,021 of federal tax, banking the $1,500 loss on Ether would save about $330, and waiting until Dec 6, 2026 to sell the newest bitcoin would save about $127.

3d31579.summary: Each spouse can now have their own health FSA, up to the yearly limit each, instead of one shared election. (An FSA is a flexible spending account: money taken from pay before tax for medical costs.) The HSA and FSA page asks for the second person's election, and the Federal estimate, Paycheck and Contribution limits pages take each FSA off that person's own pay.
points: The HSA and FSA page has a new box for the other adult's FSA election.

The FSA's tax saved now leaves out any amount over the limit. Its payroll-tax saving now counts Social Security tax only on pay up to the Social Security pay limit; before, it was a flat 7.65% of the whole election.
The Roth income check on Contribution limits no longer takes the HSA money off twice from wages typed from a W-2.
numbers: $184,500 Social Security pay limit in 2026
Before: a flat 7.65% payroll saving on the whole election

shots.caption: The HSA and FSA page with both spouses' elections: $5,800 in all (Ana $2,000, Bo $3,800, limit $3,400 each), $1,601 of tax saved, and a warning that an election is over the limit.
The form now asks for each person's FSA election separately ('Ana's FSA election' and 'Bo's FSA election'), with a note that each can put in up to the limit.

8a384e3.summary: The loss carried to next year now follows the IRS's capital loss carryover worksheet. In a year when your income is below your deductions, the whole loss now carries forward; before, only the part over $3,000 did. The Federal estimate, Capital gains, Tax report and Tax lots pages all use this one figure.
points: The carryover is worked once, the way the worksheet in IRS Publication 550 does it, and shared by every page.
Low-income years no longer lose part of the loss: when taxable income is below zero, the whole loss carries to next year.
Capital gains, the Tax report and Tax lots show the same carryover as the Federal estimate.
numbers: $3,000 of net loss a year against other income

shots.caption: The Capital gains page after adding a sample $20,000 loss: $3,000 comes off other income this year, $17,000 carries forward, and the 2026 tax drops by about $660.

5417f39.summary: This fixed a double count on the Federal estimate. Wages typed in from a W-2 already leave out the HSA money taken from pay, but the estimate took it off a second time, which made the tax look too low. The HSA and FSA page's tax saved now comes out the same whether wages are typed in or come from the Income page.
points: The W-2 wage box already leaves out HSA money taken from pay (within the limit), so it is no longer taken off again.
When the HSA page works out the return without the HSA, it adds that money back to typed wages, so its tax saved stays right.
New tests check wages typed from a W-2.

shots.caption: The Federal estimate with the sample household. 'What the plan already knows' lists wages from the Income page. A W-2 wage figure typed under 'Figures the plan cannot see' replaces them, and that typed figure is the one that no longer has the HSA money taken off twice.

The HSA and FSA page's 'tax saved' figure, about $1,054 here (a picture taken earlier the same day, just before this fix). After this fix that figure comes out the same whether wages are typed in from a W-2 or come from the Income page.

98ce1d0.summary: The Tax lots and harvesting page now agrees with its answer key on every row. ('Harvesting' means selling losing investments to cut this year's tax.) The saving shown is now what the sale really cuts this year's federal tax by: losses first cancel gains, then at most $3,000 of other income. A $40,000 loss with no gains now saves about $1,074, not the $7,520 the page used to show.
points: The page says how much of the loss carries to next year, worked the way the IRS worksheet does it.
Buying the same fund in the last 30 days, in any account including an IRA, now cancels the loss on that many shares (the wash-sale rule), and the page names the purchase.
A lot bought on February 28 before a leap year turns long-term on March 1, not February 29.
The note on leftover shares and the 'sell these first' order now describe what the page really does.
numbers: 2,000 households and 3,000 lots in the answer key
$40,000 loss: about $1,074 saved, not $7,520
$3,000 a year off other income ($1,500 filing separately)
30-day wash-sale window

shots.caption: The Tax lots page with a sample portfolio: $7,900 of losses could be harvested, but $1,200 does not count because 40 more shares of the same fund were bought in an IRA within 30 days. The harvest cuts this year's tax by about $660, and $3,700 carries to next year.
The same page without the IRA purchase: the full $7,900 counts, about $660 comes off this year's tax, and $4,900 carries to next year.

988dd0e.summary: This built the tax-lots answer key, an independent program written from the tax law without reading the app. It works 2,000 example households holding 3,000 investment purchases ('lots'), and a test compares the Tax lots and harvesting page with it. It found three causes of difference, kept as a to-do list that the next change cleared.
points: It covers short- and long-term holding periods, how losses cancel gains and other income, the carryover to next year, the wash-sale rule and the 3.8% investment-income tax.
It is built from the tax law, IRS Publication 550 and IRS rulings, never from the app's code.
It found three causes: the holding period for a February 28 purchase, the tax a harvest really saves this year, and wash sales against purchases already on file.
numbers: 2,000 households
3,000 lots
3 causes found

shots.caption: The Tax lots and harvesting page that the answer key checks, shown with the sample household's lots after the fixes that followed.

c87600e.summary: A married couple filing separately is now worked as two returns, one each, the way the IRS does it, instead of one combined return at the separate rates. Each spouse's own pay, retirement and HSA money and income go on their own return. The Federal estimate shows each return's tax, and every page that starts from the Federal estimate follows.
points: Income in neither name and figures typed on the page are split in half, the children go on the higher earner's return, and if one spouse itemizes, both must.
The Federal estimate has a new 'Two returns' card with each spouse's tax.
The Bracket explorer shows the bracket ladder of the person marked 'Me', plus both returns' brackets.
The contribution-limit and estimated-tax answer keys now agree on every row, separate filers included.
numbers: 190 separate-filing to-dos cleared from the limits answer key
3,000 households in the estimated-tax answer key

shots.caption: The Federal estimate for a sample couple filing separately: about $15,072 in all, shown as Ana's return ($8,590) and Bo's return ($6,482).
The Bracket explorer for the same couple: Ana's own ladder in the 22% bracket, with both returns listed.

7211faf.summary: This fixed the Contribution limits, HSA and FSA, and Federal estimate pages using what a new answer key for the two limit pages found, from 3,000 example households worked from the tax law. A check confirmed 25 page bugs and 3 shortcuts. All were fixed except the HSA tax saved for couples filing separately, left for the next change. Health savings account (HSA) rules, catch-up limits, the Roth IRA income check and deadlines now follow the law.
points: The 2027 HSA limits are in ($4,500 alone, $9,000 for a family). Other 2027 limits are not published yet, so they stay at 2026's.
The HSA can be marked 'no high-deductible plan', and then no HSA money is allowed. Only the person on a self-only plan can have an HSA, and spouses with family cover share one limit.

Roth 401(k) money now counts toward the 401(k) limit, and the 401(k) catch-up (the extra allowed from age 50) is capped by pay. The Roth IRA check is per person and says how much each adult can put in directly.
The IRA and HSA deadline moves off weekends and holidays: April 18, 2028 for 2027 money.
The Federal estimate takes the health FSA off pay and taxes 401(k), HSA and IRA money over its limit instead of deducting it.
numbers: 3,000 households in the answer key
25 page bugs and 3 shortcuts confirmed
2027 HSA limit: $4,500 alone, $9,000 family
April 18, 2028 deadline for 2027 IRA and HSA money

shots.caption: The Contribution limits page for the sample couple: $40,680 of room left this year in accounts with tax breaks, an HSA line for each adult (Bo has none because only Ana is on the self-only plan), and how much each can put in a Roth IRA directly.
The HSA and FSA page when 'no high-deductible plan' is chosen. It warns that the $2,500 going in saves no tax and is charged 6% a year until it is taken out.
The HSA's tax saved, about $1,054: $996 of income tax plus $58 of payroll tax. The payroll part is small because Bo earns over the Social Security pay limit.

00a086d.summary: The safety check that stops private numbers, such as account numbers, from being published in the public repo flagged two long strings of digits in the new contribution-limits answer key. They are only pieces of the digital fingerprints the key keeps of the law texts it downloaded, so they were marked as safe and the check no longer blocks the answer key.
points: The privacy check refuses any long run of digits that could be an account number
The two strings it caught are parts of fingerprints that prove which copy of a law text was read
Only those two exact strings, in the answer key's two rule files, are now allowed; everything else is still checked
numbers: 2 digit strings allowed

980cea0.summary: A new answer key for the yearly limits on what you can put into tax-advantaged accounts: 401(k)s, IRAs, health savings accounts (HSAs) and health flexible spending accounts (FSAs). It works 3,000 example households straight from the tax law and IRS notices, never from the app, and a test compares the Contribution limits and HSA and FSA pages with it. This first version records every place the pages disagree in a to-do list; the fixes came in a later change.
points: Checks the 401(k) limit and the extra 'catch-up' amount allowed from age 50, the IRA limit shared by regular and Roth IRAs, and the income limit for putting money into a Roth IRA
Checks HSA limits per person and for a family (one family limit that spouses share), and health FSA limits and carryover
Works every household two separate ways and refuses to save the results if they differ by more than a cent

Mismatches it listed include a Roth 401(k) counted against the IRA limit, an HSA limit given to someone without a qualifying health plan, a family HSA limit not shared between spouses, and missing 2027 HSA limits
numbers: 3,000 example households
29 kinds of mismatch on its to-do list
91 checks against examples worked by hand
tax years 2025 and 2026 (2027 for HSAs)

shots.caption: The Contribution limits page as this answer key first found it, before the fixes: each adult's 401(k), IRA and HSA room, the Roth IRA income limit and the deadlines.

32b5588.summary: A new answer key for the Estimated payments and Withholding check pages. It works out every quarterly tax due date for 2024 to 2027 and 3,000 example households from the tax law and the IRS form instructions, never from the app. It found five problems on the pages, all fixed, and the Withholding check's penalty warning was corrected too, so every row now agrees.
points: A quarter's status now counts everything already paid, so the page no longer shows a $0 next payment or the wrong overdue date
A payment made late still warns about the penalty for that quarter
Patriots' Day, an April holiday in Maine and Massachusetts, no longer moves the April estimated payment (it moves only the tax return's due date), on both Estimated payments and the Money calendar
In the January after the tax year, no more paychecks are counted, and a typed $0 'withheld so far' is now taken as zero instead of ignored
Also changed: the Withholding check's penalty warning uses the law's $1,000 test, which looks only at tax still owed after what your pay withholds
numbers: 3,000 example households
every due date for 2024 to 2027
5 problems fixed
$1,000 penalty test

shots.caption: Estimated payments with $9,000 already paid: the first two quarters now show 'paid', the third 'behind', and the headline asks for the $2,981 that is overdue.
The Withholding check page, the second page this answer key checks: the year's tax, what pay withholds by December, and what is still to pay.

d3db64a.summary: On the Human capital page (what your future pay is worth), the links to Life cover and Disability cover were small words inside a sentence, hard to tap on a phone. They are now full-size buttons under 'What it means'. A check of every page on a phone found this.
points: 'Life cover' and 'Disability cover' are now two outlined buttons big enough for a thumb
Found by the phone check of the whole app, where 147 of 152 pages were clean
The other pages flagged were the AI helper not running in the test copy, and the Docs page's links
numbers: 147 of 152 pages clean on the phone check

shots.caption: The Human capital page for the sample family; near the bottom, under 'What it means', are the new Life cover and Disability cover buttons.

4eb83d6.summary: The pages built before the builders split the work were checked figure by figure against their official sources, and the out-of-date or wrong ones were corrected. Changes landed on 18 pages, covering federal tax, Medicare, insurance, mortgage, retirement savings and fund figures.
points: Federal tax: a surviving spouse's child tax credit now starts shrinking above $200,000; when a married couple files separate returns, Social Security is taxed from the first dollar unless they lived apart all year, with a new 'we lived apart all year' tick; 2027 uses the Social Security pay limit of $192,300
Medicare: explains that the income surcharge lines (IRMAA, the extra premium charged on higher incomes) rise with prices every year, the top one only from 2028, and shows the 2027 drug-plan premium

Mortgage insurance is now counted from the price you paid for the home, as the law says: the page says when you can ask the lender to end it and when it ends by itself, and asks for the price if it is missing

Also updated: long-term care costs to 2025 figures, the 2027 limit on earnings while drawing Social Security early (Life insurance needs), umbrella insurance prices, a Roth 401(k) now sharing the regular 401(k) limit, the Financial independence page's years from a zero start worked with your own figures, fund fees and names, and the wording of the penalty-safe amount
numbers: 18 pages changed
22 fund fees and names updated
$192,300 Social Security pay limit for 2027
$200,000 where a surviving spouse's child credit starts shrinking

shots.caption: Federal estimate for a couple filing separately: a notice explains that Social Security is taxed from the first dollar, and 'We lived apart all year' is a new tick box under Year and people.
Medicare at 65: the note under the income surcharge table now explains that its lines rise with prices every year, the top one only from 2028.
Mortgage: the mortgage insurance card says 'you can ask to end it' and explains that the law counts from the price you paid, asking you to enter that price on Your home for the exact dates.

b8b365a.summary: A new answer key for the estate and gift tax pages works 3,500 cases from the tax code, its regulations and the IRS figures, never from the app. Every problem it found on the Gifting and Estate tax pages was fixed, so the pages now agree with it everywhere. Six pages also lost a stray word 'null' under their forms.
points: Gifting: when a couple 'splits' one gift in a year, every gift either of them made that year is now split too, as the law says, and the page says so

Gifting: gifts to a child's 529 college plan in one year count as one total, spread over five years only when it is over the yearly tax-free amount; gifts from 2011 to 2023 use their own year's limits
Estate tax: gift tax already due on big lifetime gifts now comes off the estate tax
Estate tax for a couple: works out both orders of death and shows the costlier, instead of a guess that could overstate the tax by millions
Pensions, Annuities, Expected inheritance, Digital assets, Legacy goals and Gifting no longer show the word 'null' under their forms
numbers: 3,500 cases (1,000 tax-table rows, 1,500 estates, 1,000 gift plans)
6 pages lost a stray 'null'

shots.caption: Gifting: a new note explains that a gift from both of you splits every gift that year, and the 529 gift shows as spread over five years.
Estate tax for the sample couple: the estate today, room under the exemption, and what happens at each of the two deaths.

8f0c608.summary: On the Ledger page, the way to sort uncategorised transactions was a small link inside a sentence. 'File them in a few taps' is now a full-size button in its notice, easy to hit with a thumb. The check of every page at desktop width found it.
points: 'File them in a few taps' is now an outlined button inside the '3 transactions have no category yet' notice, under the sentence
Found by the desktop check of every page
The shared board the AI builders use to coordinate was updated with this status

shots.caption: The Ledger on a phone: inside the notice that three transactions have no category, 'File them in a few taps' is now a full-size button.

710c3da.summary: The Estimated payments page (quarterly tax payments for income with no tax taken out) now moves a due date that falls on a weekend or holiday to the next business day, as the IRS allows. Late in the year it leads with what is behind and asks you to pay it now, and if you have not typed your withholding it uses the Paycheck page's estimate instead of assuming none.
points: A due date on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday moves to the next business day, using the same holiday dates as the Money calendar
2027's last payment shows January 18, 2028 instead of January 15
Late in the year the headline is the amount behind ('pay it now'), then the next payment, instead of a date that has already passed
With no withholding typed, the Paycheck page's estimate of what your pay withholds counts, with a note saying so
The Side income page and the tax report say the same
numbers: January 18, 2028 instead of January 15

shots.caption: Estimated payments: the headline says '$3,071 behind: pay it now', then the next payment, and a note says withholding is estimated from the Paycheck page.

1d0d8d8.summary: A new answer key for the health cost pages works 4,500 cases from the law and the IRS and Medicare agency tables, never from the app. The Medicare income surcharge already agreed; the 22 problems it found on Healthcare before 65 and Health plan compare were fixed, so every case now agrees.
points: Healthcare before 65: no marketplace tax credit under the poverty line, with a note that Medicaid may cover you instead; exactly 133% of the poverty line lands in the right band; the share of income is rounded the way the IRS does
Healthcare before 65: uses the federal age table's own figure for every age, counts only the three oldest children under 21, and for 2027 cover uses the poverty line and IRS table that apply to 2027
Health plan compare: uses the 2027 health savings account (HSA) limits for 2027 dates, and asks for a plan's out-of-pocket maximum before calling it HSA-eligible
Health plan compare no longer shows the word 'null' under its form
numbers: 4,500 cases (2,000 marketplace households, 1,500 Medicare surcharge cases, 1,000 high-deductible plans)
22 problems fixed

shots.caption: Healthcare before 65: the cost of cover until Medicare, the years over the tax-credit cliff, and a year-by-year list.
Health plan compare: three plans side by side for a quiet, usual and bad year, with the HSA plan's tax savings counted.

b6475c0.summary: The last re-checks of the earlier review fixes to Voice notes, Explain a page and the Plan critic found a few new slips, and each one was fixed with a test. Voice notes now reads tricky sentences correctly and asks for a day it cannot read, and Explain a page keeps more names private.
points: Voice notes no longer drops the sentence after 'Lee, Dr.' or 'Main St.', and a deposit 'with no fees' stays money in
A bill 'due to' someone is a reminder again, and 'card games' or 'savings jars' are things bought, not an account
A day it cannot read ('on Veterans Day', '2 weeks before') is asked for instead of using today
Explain a page also swaps a payee's name hidden inside a goal, income or expense name before anything goes to the AI, and treats an answer cut off mid-thought as no answer
The Plan critic's note on what the AI reads now says accounts are called by their kind and a number, such as 'credit card 1'

shots.caption: Voice notes reading a tricky note: 'Paid 150 to Lee, Dr.' becomes its own entry, the paycheck with no fees is money in, card games are money spent, and 'Veterans Day' is asked for as 'Still needed: the day'.

9fb346f.summary: A careful review of Explain a page, Voice notes and the Plan critic, covering correctness, privacy and plain language, found 84 problems; each was confirmed by a separate checker, fixed, and then re-checked. The big win is privacy: names, addresses, employers, banks and birth dates you typed no longer reach the AI.
points: Payees, people outside the household, addresses, employers, banks and insurers, surnames, the plan's name and birth dates are no longer sent to the AI; stand-ins keep the figures the same and the real names come back in the answer
Explain a page (renamed from 'Explain this page') always asks about the page you picked, names it on its button, puts the 'not checked' warning first, and says plainly what to do when the AI is off
Voice notes no longer invents an amount or a day from times, percents or counts, tells money in from money spent, and asks instead of guessing
A long voice note is read in parts and the rest stays in the box; 'Add all' keeps what you typed and catches duplicates

Voice notes turning one typed note into five entries to check; the mortgage payment is held back with 'Still needed: who it was paid to' instead of a guess.

ae52638.summary: A new answer key for the debt pages (Pay off debts, Credit cards, Mortgage) works 3,500 cases from the math and the lending rules, without reading the app. It showed that 'paying only the minimum' on a card finished too soon and too cheaply, which was fixed; the pages now agree everywhere.
points: When a card has no required payment typed, 'paying only the minimum' now takes 2% of what you owe at the start of each month (at least $25), the way federal Truth in Lending rules have card statements work it out
So the card no longer looks like it is paid off sooner and cheaper than it really would be
A card that pays off very slowly now shows how long it takes, instead of 'it never ends' after 100 years

The key also checks paying the highest rate first ('avalanche') or the smallest balance first ('snowball'), balance transfers, extra mortgage payments, paying every two weeks, re-working the loan after a lump sum (a recast) and mortgage insurance
numbers: 3,500 cases
2% of the month's opening balance
100 years

1265f56.summary: An answer key now checks the Student loans page: a separate program, written from the law and the Education Department's rules without looking at the app, works 2,000 example loans, and a test compares the page with it. The same change fixed two things on the Tax lots page (shares you bought at different times and prices), so long-term versus short-term and the tax rate on a gain now follow IRS rules more closely.
points: 2,000 example loans worked three ways: the fixed 10-year plan, income-based repayment, and the new Repayment Assistance Plan
The five places where the page and the answer key disagree are written down as a to-do list for the page
Tax lots: shares count as long-term (lower tax) the day after their first anniversary, counted on the calendar the way the IRS does, so a February 29 in between no longer makes it a day early

The Social Security Administration's October 2026 figures were added, no benefit comes out a dime low any more, and the math now also works out spouse and survivor amounts.
points: The Social Security Administration's October 2026 figures are in: the 2025 national wage index, the 3.6% cost-of-living raise from December 2026, the 2027 limit on pay that counts ($192,300) and the pay needed for one work credit in 2027 ($1,970).
The 2027 "bend points" (the income break points in the benefit formula) now come out at $1,340 and $8,077.
Years past the published table keep the last limit on pay that counts. Before, they had no limit at all.
Benefits are still rounded down to the dime, as the law says, but a tiny computer rounding error no longer knocks an exact amount down a dime.

The math now works out each person's spouse and survivor benefits (with the legal limit when the worker claimed early). For a couple it also works out the top-ups and what the survivor keeps. These amounts are not on the page yet; showing them was passed to the designer. Two mistakes found in the answer key itself were filed.
numbers: 66,000 cases checked (was a 2% sample)
3.6% raise from December 2026
2027 bend points $1,340 and $8,077
13,210 tests pass, 0 left to do

shots.caption: Social Security for the sample family: $66,600 a year in all, with Ana's monthly amount at five claiming ages from 62 to 70. The new spouse and survivor amounts are not shown yet.

f4e6bb4.summary: Three fixes. A pension typed on the Income page now counts in "Will the money last?" and in the retirement pages built on it. The federal tax math now agrees with all 12,000 answer-key returns, and the retirement pages agree with all 12,700 answer-key cases. Tests still waiting for a fix fell from 2,720 to 6, and those 6 (Social Security) were fixed next.
points: A pension typed on the Income page now counts from its start date to its end date, and keeps up with inflation if it has a yearly raise. If the same pension is also in the plan's separate pension list, it is counted once, not twice.

Federal tax: a net loss on investments of up to $3,000 now comes off any income, wages included. The extra deduction for people 65 and over works per person, and only on joint returns for married couples. The 2026 rules for charity gifts and the top-bracket limit on deductions are in.
The Federal page's 3.8% tax on investment income now counts interest, all dividends and gains.

Required withdrawals (the yearly amounts the law makes you take out of pre-tax accounts) are worked out on each person's own accounts at their own age, from 70½ for people born before July 1949. An employer's deposits now count toward the health savings account limit.

"How much can I spend" no longer stops short. Roth conversions (moving pre-tax money into an account that is tax-free later) now fill a tax bracket to the cent. "How long to plan for" no longer stops at 120.
numbers: 12,000 federal tax returns agree
12,700 retirement cases agree
Tests waiting for a fix: 2,720 before, 6 after
Investment loss of up to $3,000 against any income

shots.caption: "Will the money last?" for the sample family. The money lasts, with both partners' Social Security listed as guaranteed income.
The Federal estimate page: about $17,760 of federal tax for 2026, step by step from income to tax.
Required withdrawals: the year each partner starts, and the amount for each year after.

c341831.summary: The tools that take screenshots of the app and click through it like a person used to look only for Chrome or Edge on Windows. They now also find the Chromium browser on Linux. That means screenshots and the whole-app phone check work from a cloud session too.
points: Also tries a browser you name yourself, plus the usual Linux places for Chromium and Google Chrome.
On Linux it starts the browser in the mode that cloud machines need.
The app itself did not change.

113e0d7.summary: An answer key for federal income tax: 12,000 made-up tax returns for 2024, 2025 and 2026, worked out from the IRS's own figures without looking at the app. A test compares the Federal estimate page's math with every one, to within $1. At first the app got 2,246 of them wrong. Those were kept as to-do tests, sorted by cause, and were all fixed four days later.
points: 4,000 returns for each of 2024, 2025 and 2026. The rules were written up from the IRS's yearly tables and the 2025 tax law.
Every answer must match within $1.

The 2,246 misses by cause: the 2026 charity rules (998); investment losses dropped when they were bigger than other non-wage income (870); the extra deduction for people 65 and over given on married-filing-separately returns, where the law does not allow it (325), and how it shrinks per person (96); the 2026 limit on deductions in the top bracket (225); the state-and-local tax cap on separate returns (50); and one line of the capital-gains worksheet (1). Some returns had more than one cause, so these add up to more than 2,246.
Each cause has a worked example in the written rules, so whoever fixes it can follow the law step by step.
numbers: 12,000 made-up returns
2,246 the app got wrong at first
Each within $1

shots.caption: The Federal estimate page the answer key checks: about $17,760 of federal tax for 2026 for the sample family, step by step from income to tax.

e197072.summary: A new page puts a value on all the pay each earner still has to earn before retiring, in today's money, and sets it beside what the household has saved. It shows what share of everything you have is pay still to come, and why that makes life and disability insurance matter.
points: Each earner's pay up to retirement is valued in today's money, before and after tax. A less steady job counts for less: a steady job is valued at the bond return, an average one at 2 points more, a volatile one at the stock return.
Flags any earner with no life insurance, because the household would lose that pay if they died.
A chart shows pay still to come shrinking as savings grow, and marks the year savings overtake it.
Explains what this means: protect it with insurance, invest around it, and how much raises one point bigger would add.
numbers: An average job is valued at the bond return plus 2 points

shots.caption: The sample couple's future pay is worth about $3.16 million in today's money, 78% of everything they have, and the chart marks the year savings overtake it.
The 'How steady is each job?' section opened, where you pick steady, average or volatile for each earner.

0ecb6b9.summary: The Home page now shows what the house is worth, how much of it is yours, what it costs to keep each year, and what you would walk away with if you sold today. It also looks ahead 5, 10 and 20 years and keeps a history each time you update the value.
points: The home's value, your share after the mortgage, and how much it has grown since you bought it.
A year of costs: property tax, insurance, association dues, upkeep and mortgage interest. The part of the payment that pays down the loan is shown separately, because that money becomes yours.
Selling today: selling costs, paying off the mortgage, and tax only on any gain above the amount that is tax-free on a main home ($250,000, or $500,000 for a married couple filing together).
Value and equity in 5, 10 and 20 years, following the mortgage page's schedule. Updating the value keeps the old ones as history.
numbers: $250,000 tax-free gain on a main home ($500,000 for a married couple filing together)
Looks ahead 5, 10 and 20 years

shots.caption: The sample house is worth $380,000, $115,000 of it is yours, it costs $26,853 a year to keep, and selling today would leave $92,200.

18c0f61.summary: The Vehicles page adds up what each car really costs per year and per mile, not just the payment. It compares keeping the car with buying new or leasing over the same years, and marks the cheapest.
points: Yearly cost: value lost, fuel or charging, insurance, upkeep, registration and loan interest, plus a cost per mile.
Keep, buy new or lease over the same number of years: what you would pay, minus what the car is still worth at the end.
If you owe more on the loan than the car is worth (an 'upside-down' loan), the comparison pays that off first.
Works for electric cars too, counting charging instead of fuel.
numbers: Assumes the car you have loses 12% of its value a year unless you change it

shots.caption: A sedan costs $6,071 a year ($0.55 a mile), and over five years keeping it is $18,302 cheaper than the next-best choice, buying new.
Before any car is added: what the page does, and the form to add one.

f6ff7c2.summary: A new page plans any big purchase, from a sofa to a boat, three ways: save up by a date, buy now on a payment plan, or pay cash. Each way is checked against the money left over each month. When that money runs short, the page shows which savings goals would slow down.
points: Save up: the monthly amount that reaches the price by the date you want, counting the interest your savings earn along the way.
Finance now: a level payment, 0% for the whole time, or 0% for a while and then the rate, with the total interest shown.
Pay cash: how much cash would be left, with a warning if that falls below your emergency fund target.
If the monthly amount is more than you have left over, goals give way least important first, either paused or pushed back by a number of months.

shots.caption: A $3,000 sofa with $1,000 already set aside: save $283 a month until June 2027, pay $185 a month on a plan, or pay cash and drop below the emergency target.
Before you name a purchase, the page shows a $3,000 example and the form to fill in.

095b122.summary: The Renovation page weighs what a home project costs against how much it adds to the home's price, and compares four ways to pay for it. The ways to pay are ranked by how much extra each really costs, in today's money.
points: The value added comes from national 2024 averages for common projects (rounded), or from your own figure.
Four ways to pay: cash from savings, a home-equity line of credit, a cash-out refinance (a new, bigger mortgage) and a personal loan.
Each is ranked by how much more it costs than paying cash, counting what the money could have earned in the meantime at the plan's return.
Shows the cash cushion you would have left and how much could be borrowed against the home.
numbers: National 2024 averages for the value each project adds
4 ways to pay compared

shots.caption: A $30,000 kitchen refresh adds about $28,500 of value; with not enough cash to pay outright, a home-equity line is the cheapest way, and all four ways are listed.

1be9b54.summary: The Rental analysis page follows each rental property from the rent coming in to the cash left after tax, and runs the checks a lender would make. It also shows how much the rental adds to your wealth as the loan shrinks and the value grows.
points: The year line by line: rent, an allowance for empty months, running costs, income after costs, loan payments split into interest and principal, then tax.

Investor yardsticks in plain words: the yearly return on the property's value (cap rate), the return on the cash you put in (cash-on-cash), whether the rent comfortably covers the loan, and how full the property must be to break even.
Tax: the building is written off over 27.5 years (depreciation), and the up-to-$25,000 yearly allowance for rental losses is shared across all your rentals.
What it adds to your wealth: the cash, the loan paid down and the growth in value. You can add, change and remove rentals.
numbers: Building written off over 27.5 years
Up to $25,000 of rental losses a year can count against other income (less once income passes $100,000)

shots.caption: A sample duplex leaves $6,940 of cash a year before tax, a 6.5% yearly return on its value (cap rate), shown with the year line by line, the lender's checks and the tax.

2290b4f.summary: The Employer stock page shows how much of your savings rides on the company you work for, counting shares held anywhere, vested options and grants still to come. Your pay depends on the same company, so the page shows what a bad year would take and how to bring the stake down.
points: Adds up company shares in every account, vested options and grants still to vest, and compares the total with the usual ceiling of 10% of invested wealth.
Shows what a halving of the share price would cost while your job depends on the same company.
Lists the next year's vests and whether the 22% your employer holds back for federal tax covers your real tax rate.
How to get under 10%: sell the shares inside the retirement plan first, because that costs no tax.
numbers: 10% usual ceiling for one company
22% federal tax held back on vesting shares

shots.caption: A sample ACME stake: $250,000 and 63% of invested wealth, about $165,000 lost if the price halved, the vests coming up, and how far selling the shares would bring it down (to 55% here, because of grants still to vest).
Before any company is entered: what the page is for, and where to start.

390ff2f.summary: The Help page explains how the app works in plain words and walks a newcomer through seven first steps, ticking each one the plan already covers. It also has a search over every page, lists every page by section, and answers common questions.
points: A short explanation in plain words of how the app works.
Seven first steps (the people in the household, what you own and owe, income, spending, each debt's rate and payment, goals, retirement saving), each ticked once the plan has it.
A search box: type what you want to do, such as 'pay off the card', and it finds the right pages, ranked the same way as the menu's search.
Every page by section, saying what it is for and which are still coming, plus the questions people ask.
numbers: 7 first steps

shots.caption: 5 of the 7 first steps done for the sample family, every section of pages, and the questions people ask.
Typing 'pay off the card' finds three pages: Income, Debts and Pay off debts.

daf24ed.summary: The Crypto page brings together coins held in crypto accounts and bitcoin or ether funds held anywhere else. It shows what they are worth against what you paid, their share of your net worth, how much a crash like 2018's or 2022's would take, and the tax if you sold today.
points: Value against cost, with a flag when crypto is more than 5% of your net worth.
What a 75% fall would take, based on bitcoin's drops of 2018 and 2022.
Each coin's separate purchases, with a quick box to update the price.

The tax if sold today, purchase by purchase. It also shows losses worth taking now (the rule that cancels a tax loss when you buy the same thing back soon does not apply to coins you hold directly) and gains worth holding a little longer for the lower rate.
You can add a coin, and the account's balance follows its coins.
numbers: Flagged above 5% of net worth
What a 75% fall would take

shots.caption: Sample crypto: $16,160, just over 5% of net worth, a 75% fall would take $11,520, each coin with a price box, and the tax if everything were sold.
Before any coin is added: what the page does, and the form to add one.

34744f1.summary: A new printable page sets out a year of the household's money the way a business reports its cash: what living brings in after tax, what goes into investments, and what goes to loans. The three parts add up to the cash left over, and up to the last twelve months from your bank files sit beside them.
points: Living: pay and other income, minus taxes and living costs.
Investing: your own money put into retirement, health and brokerage accounts. The employer's match is noted but not counted, because it never passes through your bank.
Debts: loan payments split into interest and paying down what you owe. Mortgage or loan payments listed among your expenses are moved here so they are not counted twice.
Up to the last twelve complete months from imported bank files, leaving out transfers between your own accounts. The page prints or saves as a PDF.
numbers: Up to the last 12 complete months from the bank files

shots.caption: The sample family's year: $94,856 from living, $33,480 to loans and cards, $61,376 left in cash, with the two months of bank files so far below.

51fcf82.summary: A new printable balance sheet lists everything you own by how fast it turns into cash, and what each thing would really bring if cashed in today. Debts are split into what is due within a year and what comes later. The sheet also splits everything by owner and explains a few ratios in plain words.
points: Four groups: cash you can use today, investments you can sell in a few days, money saved for later (retirement, health and college accounts) that can carry tax or a penalty if taken out early, and a home or cars that take months to sell.
'If cashed in' takes off income tax and the 10% early-withdrawal penalty before age 59½ on pre-tax retirement money, and about 6% selling costs on a home.
Debts due within a year (a card's whole balance, plus the part of each loan the next twelve payments pay off) and debts due later.
A split by owner, plus ratios: months of cash, cash and investments against what falls due within a year, what you owe against what you own, and the invested share.
numbers: 4 groups by how fast things turn into cash
10% early-withdrawal penalty before age 59½
About 6% to sell a home

shots.caption: The sample couple's sheet: $1,000,200 net worth, $765,560 if everything were sold today, what they own grouped by how fast it turns into cash, and what the numbers say.

086389d.summary: The Net worth projection page now works. It shows what the household will be worth at the end of each year, up to five years past retirement, in today's money. It adds up the savings forecast from the Retirement page, the home growing in value, cars losing value, college savings growing and debts shrinking on the payoff plan.
points: A line chart of net worth, with retirement and the year the mortgage (or all debt) is paid off marked on it.
Milestones along the way: the mortgage paid off, net worth doubling, passing a million, the highest point.
Every five years, what the total is made of: savings and investments, the home, and what is still owed.
"Today's money" takes rising prices out, so a figure 30 years away can be compared with what money buys now.
numbers: Homes grow 3.5% a year unless you change it
Cars lose 15% a year unless you change it
Looks ahead to five years past retirement: at least 10 years, at most 40
6 new tests

shots.caption: The sample family's net worth climbs to a peak around retirement. Below it are the year the mortgage is gone and what the total is made of every five years.

e77e752.summary: The State page now estimates this year's state income tax from the best information in the plan: a rate you type, last year's state return, or your state's own 2026 flat rate. It also shows how much counting that tax on the federal return would save, what is still owed after withholding, and what the same income would pay in other states.
points: Knows the states that do not tax wages at all and the states that charge one flat rate.
If you enter last year's state return, it takes the share of income that return took and applies it to this year.
One button adds the state tax to the federal estimate as a deduction. This only helps if you itemize (list your deductions instead of taking the standard amount).
Shows the same income in each no-tax and flat-tax state.
numbers: 9 states with no tax on wages
13 flat-rate states
10 new tests

shots.caption: The sample family moved to Illinois: about $7,436 of state tax and $620 a month to set aside, with a button to count it on the federal return and what is left after withholding.
In Texas the page just says there is no state income tax, so there is nothing to set aside.

a21e75b.summary: The Tax documents checklist now builds your list of tax forms straight from the plan: a wage statement (W-2) for each person with a job, the bank's interest form, the brokerage statement, the mortgage form, pension and Social Security forms, and so on. The forms are grouped by when they should arrive, and you tick each one as it comes in.
points: Each form says who sends it and why it is on the list, for example "listed because you have a mortgage".
Grouped by arrival date: by January 31, by February 15 and by May 31.
Ticks are kept separately for each tax year, so next year starts with a clean list.
You can add documents of your own, such as receipts or statements.
numbers: Return due April 15
Interest under $10 gets no form but is still taxed
7 new tests

shots.caption: The sample family's 2026 checklist, 0 of 10 received: wage forms for both earners, plus bank, mortgage and brokerage forms, grouped by when each arrives.

e64a4e3.summary: The Consolidation page now compares rolling high-interest debts into one. The options are a personal loan, a 0% balance-transfer card, or a home-equity line (a loan backed by your house), set against paying as you do now. For each one it shows the monthly payment, the time until you are debt-free, the interest and fees, which costs least, and the risks.
points: By default it picks the debts charging 10% or more; you can choose others.
Warns when a balance transfer would not be paid off before the interest-free months end, and says what monthly payment would clear it.
Warns that with a home-equity line, card debt becomes debt your house is on the hook for.
Reminds you it only works if the cards stay paid off.
numbers: Debts at 10% or more
Example offers: a 12% personal loan with a 5% fee, a 0% card with a 4% fee, an 8.5% home-equity line
4 new tests

shots.caption: A $6,400 credit card and a $14,200 car loan ($20,600 in all) compared four ways. The 0% balance-transfer card costs least, with a warning that it will not be cleared in the free months.

ecaff7a.summary: The Student loans page now compares the ways to repay federal student loans on the household's own income. The four ways are the standard 10-year plan, income-based repayment, the new Repayment Assistance Plan, and, for public-service workers, Public Service Loan Forgiveness. It works month by month and shows each payment, how long it lasts, what is paid and forgiven, the tax on what is forgiven, and a cost in today's money that ranks them.
points: Income-based payments follow your pay as it grows and are worked out again each year.
Includes the new Repayment Assistance Plan, open to new loans from July 1, 2026.
Counts the 2026 change: loan debt that is forgiven is taxed as income again. Public-service forgiveness stays tax-free.
Ranks the plans by cost in today's money, because money you pay later is worth less than money you pay now.
numbers: Standard plan: 120 monthly payments
Repayment Assistance Plan: 1% to 10% of income, minus $50 a month per child
Public service forgiveness after 120 qualifying payments
6 new tests

shots.caption: A sample $38,000 federal loan compared plan by plan. The standard 10-year plan is cheapest in today's money, and the 2026 rules are listed below.

6e8de65.summary: The Filing status page now compares a married couple's federal tax filed jointly with the same couple filing two real separate returns. For a single parent it compares head of household with filing single. It names the cheapest way and lists what filing separately gives up.
points: The separate returns are built properly: each spouse's own pay and retirement saving, half of what is shared, and the children on the higher earner's return.
Head of household is a lower-tax status for a single parent who pays for a home. The page compares it with filing single.
Lists what separate filers lose: the student loan interest deduction, the education and child-care credits, and the Roth IRA above $10,000 of income.
Says when filing separately can pay off: large medical bills, or a student loan payment that is based on income.
numbers: Roth IRA closed above $10,000 of income when filing separately
4 new tests

shots.caption: The sample couple pays the same $17,760 whether they file jointly or separately, with a list of what filing separately would give up.

925502d.summary: The Self-employment page now shows the extra tax a side business brings. That means self-employment tax (the Social Security and Medicare an employer would otherwise pay half of), the half of it that comes off your income, the 20% business deduction, and income tax on the rest. It also shows how much of each extra $100 you keep, how much you could shelter in a SEP-IRA or solo 401(k) (retirement accounts for people who work for themselves), and the quarterly payments to make.
points: Social Security tax stops at the 2026 pay limit, and pay from a day job counts toward that limit first.
Includes the extra 0.9% Medicare tax on high earners.
Retirement room: a SEP-IRA can take 20% of the profit after half the self-employment tax, and a solo 401(k) adds your own contribution on top.
Shows what to pay each quarter, or how much more to have taken out of a day job's paycheck instead.
numbers: Self-employment tax is charged on 92.35% of the profit
$184,500 Social Security pay limit for 2026
20% business deduction
Solo 401(k) up to $72,000 in all

shots.caption: A $7,200 photography profit adds $2,195 of tax and $70 of each extra $100 is kept. Quarterly payments and retirement room are shown below.

57a40ce.summary: The Giving page now shows what a year's gifts to charity save in federal tax under the 2026 rules, and what they really cost after that saving. It also checks three ways to give the same and pay less: bunching several years of gifts into one year, giving shares that have grown instead of cash, and giving straight from an IRA after age 70½.
points: Uses the app's full federal tax calculation, not a rule of thumb.
From 2026, people who take the standard deduction can still deduct cash gifts up to $1,000 ($2,000 for a couple).
Shows whether bunching helps or ends up costing more.
Estimates the capital gains tax (tax on an investment's growth) you avoid by giving grown shares.
numbers: Up to $1,000 of cash gifts ($2,000 for a couple) deductible without itemizing
Gifts count only above 0.5% of income for those who itemize
4 new tests

shots.caption: Giving $3,000 a year saves $440 in tax. Bunching would cost about $880 more, and giving grown shares avoids about $225 of tax.

7ea45d0.summary: The Travel and events page now prices trips, weddings and other big days from their parts (flights, nights, meals, guests). It shows what to put aside each month to pay in cash by the date, and one tap turns an event into a goal that stays linked to it. Events are kept in a new list of their own in your plan; nothing already there changes.
points: A trip: flights per person, lodging per night, food per person per day, activities and other costs.
A wedding: number of guests and the main costs (venue, clothes, photos, rings).
The monthly amount counts money already saved in the linked goal.
Events whose date has passed drop out of the monthly total.
numbers: 4 new tests

shots.caption: A sample lake week priced at $4,260 from its parts and a $2,500 birthday party: $632 a month to set aside for both, each with a "Make it a goal" button.

479fe60.summary: The Vehicle page now plans the next car two ways: paying cash by the target date, or borrowing whatever is not saved by then. It shows the monthly saving needed, what you will have saved at your current pace, and the loan, payment and interest. It also checks the purchase against the 20/4/10 rule of thumb.
points: Uses the car goal from the Goals page, or a car you type in.
Adds sales tax to the price and takes off any trade-in.
Works out the loan payment and total interest for the part you have not saved.
20/4/10 rule: at least 20% down, a loan of no more than 4 years, and car costs under 10% of income before tax.
numbers: Unless you change them: 6% sales tax and a 7% loan over 5 years
3 new tests

shots.caption: A $26,790 car by March 2029: save $860 a month to pay cash, or take a $320-a-month loan. Below are the 20/4/10 checks.

59fffd2.summary: The Emergency fund page under Goals now says how many months of must-pay bills this household should keep and why. It also shows how close the cushion is to its target, when it will be full, and where to keep it. It adds a tick box that marks the emergency goal as the fund itself. The other Emergency fund page, under Assets and debts, which counts the cash you can use, now respects that tick. Nothing changes until someone ticks it.
points: Suggests 3 months with two steady earners and 6 with one, plus 3 more when pay goes up and down.
A progress bar against the target, and the date the fund will be full at the goal's monthly pace.
Where to keep it: high-yield savings, not stocks. It also shows what spare money sitting in checking could earn.
The tick answers an open question from testing: until now, money saved for the emergency goal did not count toward the cushion. Whether to use it is still the owner's call.
numbers: Suggests 3, 6 or 9 months of must-pay bills
Target: 6 months unless you change it
5 new tests

shots.caption: The sample family has $4,200 against a $31,670 target, full in about 65 months. Below is the "This goal is my emergency fund" tick.
The other Emergency fund page, which counts the cash you can use. Once the tick is on, it counts the goal's money as the cushion. Here it is off, so $11,500 stays set aside for goals.

e470868.summary: The Goal prioritiser page now shares the money left each month across the household's goals: must-haves first, then wants, then nice-to-haves, with the nearest date first in each group. It shows each goal's monthly amount against what it needs, which goals arrive on time and how late the rest would be. One button copies those amounts to the Goals page.
points: The monthly money comes from the Next best action page (what is left of pay after tax, spending and retirement saving, plus what already goes to goals), or from a figure you set.
Goals with no date get what is left: up to a twelfth of what they still need each month.
When money runs short, it shows which goals wait and by how many months.
The "Use these amounts" button sets each goal's monthly saving on the Goals page.
numbers: 4 new tests

shots.caption: $5,515 a month for goals: the emergency fund, the car, college and a Japan trip all arrive on time, with $2,323 left over.

da74d6a.summary: A review of the Employer stock page found that the tax on your next stock vests ignored the vests earlier in the same year, so a December vest was taxed as if it were the year's first pay. Now the year's earlier vests come first, each tax year's shortfall or refund is shown on its own, and the state's share always shows.
points: Vests already received this year are counted first, so a later vest is taxed at the bracket you have really reached, and the 37% withholding past $1 million of bonus-type pay counts them too.
Each calendar year gets its own sentence: what to set aside by April 15 for that year's return, or what comes back. Withholding in one year cannot pay another year's tax.
The state's share is the state's rate on the vests themselves (Illinois's 4.95% even with no other income), shown whatever the federal figure.
A child is never taken as the person who works there, and pay with no one named, or wages typed on the Federal estimate, count toward the 0.9% Medicare withholding.
Filing separately, selling company shares goes on the return of the person whose account holds them, and this year's sale is stacked on this year's vests.
numbers: $35,900 owed on a December vest after $300,000 of earlier vests (it was shown as $23,364)

75c38a8.summary: The app opens in under a second. Every open used to fetch all 529 of the app's files again, so the phone showed 'Opening your plan...' for about 4.4 seconds each time.
points: The PC told the browser to fetch every file again on each open and gave it no way to check whether anything had changed. Opening the app again was as slow as the very first time: 529 requests and 3.4 MB.

Now the PC gives each code file an address that carries a fingerprint of its contents, and lets the browser keep it. An open after the first asks the PC only for the small starting page: 2 requests, 1 KB, about 0.7 seconds.
When a file changes, its address changes too, so the next open picks up the update. The browser never mixes old and new code.
Files now travel compressed, so even the very first open downloads less than half as much (1.5 MB).

d5c61d4.summary: Three rounds of checked fixes for freelancers' tax, a raise that starts later, Social Security amounts and goals waiting their turn.
points: The Forecast takes each estimated-tax quarter out on the IRS's own date. A tax bill you type, or a payment the bank shows, now pays the earliest quarter it can, so paying the 1st quarter on April 1 no longer leaves 'April 15: 1st quarter due' on screen.

A raise from a later date keeps one record, so the careful 'count on' figure, the months you typed and Get started's pay question follow both halves: no year of pay in one lump, and no figure coming back on the raise's date.
Social Security's full-age amount comes from the earnings record, not from what an early claim pays, so what a widow keeps and a spouse's top-up are right. Saving with nothing changed writes nothing.
A goal waiting its turn is measured month by month from that turn: one that cannot be reached then reads behind, never 'about $0 a month is needed'.
